Scientists successfully transfer longevity gene and extend lifespan

Scientists borrowed a longevity secret from naked mole rats â and used it to make mice healthier and live longer. Date:

May 10, 2026

Source:

University of Rochester

Summary:

Scientists at the University of Rochester pulled off a remarkable experiment: they transferred a longevity-related gene from the famously long-lived naked mole rat into mice, and the mice ended up healthier and lived longer. The special gene boosts production of a substance called high molecular weight hyaluronic acid, which appears to protect against cancer, reduce inflammation, and support healthier aging. The modified mice showed stronger resistance to tumors, healthier guts, and lower levels of age-related inflammation. Share:

FULL STORY

Naked mole rats are not much to look at, but their biology has made them one of the most fascinating animals in aging research. These small, wrinkled rodents can live for decades, rarely develop cancer, and seem unusually protected from many of the diseases that normally arrive with age.

These small, wrinkled rodents can live for decades, rarely develop cancer, and seem unusually protected from many of the diseases that normally arrive with age. Researchers at the University of Rochester showed that one of those biological advantages can be moved into another mammal. By transferring a gene linked to the naked mole rat's unusually high levels of high molecular weight hyaluronic acid (HMW-HA), the team improved health and modestly extended lifespan in mice. The work, published in

Nature

in 2023, suggested that at least some longevity traits that evolved in long-lived animals may be adaptable beyond the species that developed them. The genetically modified mice lived healthier lives and had an approximate 4.4 percent increase in median lifespan compared with ordinary mice. "Our study provides a proof of principle that unique longevity mechanisms that evolved in long-lived mammalian species can be exported to improve the lifespans of other mammals," says Vera Gorbunova, the Doris Johns Cherry Professor of biology and medicine at Rochester. Gorbunova, along with Andrei Seluanov, a professor of biology, and their colleagues, focused on a gene that helps produce HMW-HA.

This substance is abundant in naked mole rats and has been tied to their striking resistance to cancer, inflammation, and age-related decline. Why Naked Mole Rats Fascinate Aging Scientists

Naked mole rats are about the size of mice, yet their lifespans are extraordinary for rodents. They can live up to 41 years, nearly ten times longer than similarly sized rodents. Their long lives are not the only reason scientists study them. As they age, naked mole rats appear to avoid many conditions that commonly affect other mammals, including neurodegeneration, cardiovascular disease, arthritis, and cancer. For decades, Gorbunova, Seluanov, and other researchers have been investigating how these animals stay so resilient. One major clue is HMW-HA. Naked mole rats carry roughly ten times more of it than mice and humans. In earlier work, researchers found that when HMW-HA was removed from naked mole rat cells, those cells became more likely to form tumors. That finding raised a powerful question. If HMW-HA helps naked mole rats resist cancer and age-related damage, could the same mechanism work in a different animal?

finding raised a powerful question. If HMW-HA helps naked mole rats resist cancer and age-related damage, could the same mechanism work in a different animal? Transferring a Naked Mole Rat Longevity Gene

To test the idea, the Rochester team engineered mice to carry the naked mole rat version of the hyaluronan synthase 2 gene. This gene helps make the protein that produces HMW-HA. All mammals have a version of hyaluronan synthase 2, but the naked mole rat version appears to be especially active. It seems to drive stronger gene expression, leading to greater production of the protective molecule. The modified mice developed higher levels of hyaluronan in several tissues. They also showed stronger protection against spontaneous tumors and chemically induced skin cancer. The effects were not limited to cancer resistance. The mice carrying the naked mole rat gene stayed healthier overall, lived longer than regular mice, had less inflammation in multiple tissues as they aged, and maintained better gut health. Because chronic inflammation is one of the major biological features of aging, the reduction in inflammation was especially important.

The researchers believe HMW-HA may work partly by directly influencing the immune system, although more research is needed to explain exactly how it produces such broad benefits. A Small Lifespan Gain With Big Implications

The increase in median lifespan was about 4.4 percent, which is modest. But the larger significance is that a longevity mechanism from one mammal was successfully transferred to another. That makes the finding more than a mouse study about a single gene. It supports the idea that nature's long-lived species may contain biological tools that can be studied, adapted, and possibly used to improve health in other animals. "It took us 10 years from the discovery of HMW-HA in the naked mole rat to showing that HMW-HA improves health in mice," Gorbunova says. "Our next goal is to transfer this benefit to humans."

The researchers believe there may be two main ways to pursue that goal. One would be to slow the breakdown of HMW-HA in the body. Another would be to increase its production.

main ways to pursue that goal. One would be to slow the breakdown of HMW-HA in the body. Another would be to increase its production. "We already have identified molecules that slow down hyaluronan degradation and are testing them in pre-clinical trials," Seluanov says. "We hope that our findings will provide the first, but not the last, example of how longevity adaptations from a long-lived species can be adapted to benefit human longevity and health."

Newer Research Adds to the Naked Mole Rat Story

Since the 2023

Nature

study, naked mole rats have continued to offer new clues about why they age so differently from other mammals. A 2025 study in

Science

reported another potential longevity mechanism involving cGAS, a protein better known for its role in immune defense. In humans and mice, cGAS can interfere with some forms of DNA repair, but the naked mole rat version appears to help cells repair DNA damage more effectively. That study found that specific changes in the naked mole rat protein improved genome stability and delayed signs of aging in experimental models. This newer work does not replace the HMW-HA finding. Instead, it strengthens a broader pattern.

Naked mole rats likely owe their unusually long, healthy lives to several overlapping defenses, including cancer resistance, inflammation control, DNA repair, and tissue protection. For human aging research, that matters. A single molecule is unlikely to become a simple fountain of youth. But each discovery gives scientists another possible route for targeting the biological processes that drive age-related disease. The 2023 gene transfer study remains a striking proof of concept. A survival strategy that evolved in one of nature's strangest mammals helped mice resist disease, age more smoothly, and live longer. The next challenge is determining whether those same biological tricks can be safely adapted to improve human healthspan. RELATED TOPICS

content_chunks.text: Advancements in gene therapy have achieved significant milestones in treating human diseases, offering renewed hope to patients with limited options. Key to this progress are vectors, which include both viral and non-viral methodologies that impact the success of gene therapy. Over the past two decades, three widely used viral vectors-lentiviruses (LV), adenoviruses (Ad), and adeno-associated viruses (AAV)-have enabled notable preclinical and clinical successes, including the approval of Luxturna for a genetic retinal disease and CAR-T therapies for blood cancers. Recently, the first-in-human dual AAV therapy for hereditary hearing loss, which overcomes large gene delivery, has showcased the restoration of auditory function for patients. Additionally, non-viral vectors such as lipid nanoparticles (LNP) and N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) have led to successful gene therapy products. This review focuses on both viral and non-viral delivery systems in gene therapy, highlighting their current state and future perspectives in treating human diseases.

Advancements in Gene Therapy- Current Trends and Future Directions

Gene therapy has come a long way in the last several years, transforming treatment modalities and providing hope to those suffering from genetic disorders. Gene therapy is a potentially revolutionary treatment option for diseases resulting from genetic variations. The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) of the United States has approved gene therapy products for a number of illnesses, such as sickle cell disease, cancer, hemophilia, and spinal muscular atrophy. Even with these developments, most people can still only get gene therapy through clinical trials, which emphasizes the need for continued research and development to make these cutting-edge medicines available to a wider range of patients. Current Gene Therapy Trends

Recent developments in gene therapy hold the potential to revolutionize the management of complicated diseases, malignancies, and genetic disorders. With the development of CRISPR-Cas9 technology, gene editing has become much more accurate, effective, and user-friendly, revolutionizing gene therapy. With the use of this instrument, genetic mutations that result in disease can be corrected by directly altering DNA sequences. With its enhanced selectivity and decreased off-target effects, CRISPR-Cas9 is now a mainstay of gene therapy research. Vectors of the Adeno-Associated Virus (AAV)

AAV vectors’ safety profile and capacity to target a variety of tissues have made them the go-to delivery method for gene treatments. The effectiveness of treatments has increased due to advancements in AAV vector engineering, which have increased their capacity to deliver larger genetic payloads and strengthened their selectivity for certain cell types. CAR-T Cell Treatment

Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) are two hematologic malignancies that have showed extraordinary response to Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy.

lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) and diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) are two hematologic malignancies that have showed extraordinary response to Chimeric Antigen Receptor T-cell (CAR-T) therapy. CAR-T therapy, which works by genetically altering a patient’s T cells to identify and destroy cancer cells, has shown remarkable rates of remission and is still being improved to increase efficacy and minimize adverse effects. Methods of Gene Silencing

In order to silence genes that cause harm, two essential methods for gene silencing are antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) and RNA interference (RNAi). These approaches have shown promise in treating a range of genetic illnesses, as seen by their effective application in treating conditions including transthyretin amyloidosis and spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). Gene therapy and regenerative medicine

There are now more options for treating degenerative disorders because to the combination of gene therapy and regenerative medicine. There is promise for disorders like Parkinson’s disease, heart failure, and spinal cord injuries thanks to the exploration of techniques like gene editing in conjunction with stem cell therapy, which can restore damaged tissues and organs.

Gene therapy has enormous potential, however there are still a number of obstacles to overcome:

Delivery Efficiency

: One of the biggest challenges is to ensure that therapeutic genes are expressed steadily in the target cells. The goal of current research is to create delivery systems that are more focused and efficient. Immune Response:

By targeting the vectors used to transfer genetic material, the immune system may provide a barrier to gene therapy. Important areas of continuing study include methods to enhance vector stealth and regulate the immune response. Concerns with Ethics and Regulations:

There is much discussion on the moral implications of gene editing, especially with regard to germline modifications. In order to address these worries and guarantee the security and effectiveness of gene therapy therapies, regulatory frameworks are changing. Cost and Accessibility:

Gene therapies are expensive, which prevents their general acceptance. Attempts are in progress to create more affordable production methods and broaden the availability of these transformative therapies.

Next-Generation Editing of Genomes

Even more precise than CRISPR-Cas9 are cutting edge technologies like base editing and prime editing. By directly correcting point mutations without causing double-strand breaks, these methods lower the possibility of inadvertent genetic changes. Individualized Gene Therapy

Technological developments in genomic sequencing and bioinformatics are opening the door to customized gene therapies based on a patient’s genetic composition. This strategy promises to lessen side effects and increase therapeutic efficacy. Editing the Epigenome

Changing the epigenetic markers that control gene expression without changing the underlying DNA sequence is known as epigenome editing. This strategy may be used to treat illnesses including some malignancies and neurological conditions that are associated with epigenetic dysregulation. Gene Editing in Vivo

It is becoming more and more possible to execute genetic adjustments inside the patient’s body, a process known as “in vivo gene editing.” This method could increase the number of conditions that can be treated while also streamlining the process of treatment.

Combining gene therapy with small molecule medications, biologics, and immunotherapy may improve the effectiveness of treatment. Combination treatments, which target many pathways at once, may be able to handle complicated disorders more successfully. Case Studies: Gene Therapy Success Stories

1. For Retinal Dystrophy, Luxturna

A ground-breaking gene therapy for RPE65-mediated hereditary retinal degeneration is called Luxturna (voretigene neparvovec-rzyl). Luxturna helps individuals who might otherwise experience progressive blindness by directly delivering a functioning copy of the RPE65 gene to retinal cells. 2. Spinal muscular atrophy with zolgensma

A ground-breaking gene therapy called Zolgensma (onasemnogene abeparvovec) treats the debilitating genetic condition known as spinal muscular atrophy (SMA). The SMN1 gene is replaced by this therapy, which is a one-time treatment that has significantly increased the motor function and survival of sick infants. 3. Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia with Kymriah

The treatment landscape for pediatric and young adult patients with relapsed or refractory B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) has been completely changed by the CAR-T cell therapy known as Kymriah (tisagenlecleucel).

Embracing the Potential of Gene Therapy

In terms of medical innovation, gene therapy is at the forefront, providing patients with previously incurable illnesses with new hope. Recent developments in genome editing, vector engineering, and regenerative medicine have propelled the area forward tremendously.

Notwithstanding these obstacles, gene therapy appears to have a bright future ahead of it, with further research poised to increase the number of diseases that can be treated and enhance treatment results. In order to fully utilize gene therapy and enhance patient care, healthcare practitioners must stay up to date on these advancements.

Medical science is evolving faster than ever, and one field leading the way is

gene replacement therapy

. For decades, doctors treated illnesses by managing symptoms. Now, medicine is moving toward repairing the very roots of disease — our genes. This shift explains why gene replacement therapy is often called a buzzword in healthcare. In this guide, we’ll explore what it means, how it works, and why experts, including Manaaki Healthcare, see it as a game-changer for patients worldwide. What is Gene Replacement Therapy? Gene replacement therapy is a technique where faulty or missing genes are replaced with healthy ones. Genes carry instructions for how our bodies function. When these instructions are flawed, diseases like muscular dystrophy, cystic fibrosis, and certain cancers can develop. By replacing the defective gene, doctors aim to restore normal function. Instead of treating only symptoms, this therapy targets the root cause. Why It’s Gaining Attention

Targeting the Cause, Not Just Symptoms

Unlike traditional treatments that manage outward effects, gene replacement therapy works at the genetic level. This is a major reason it’s drawing global attention.

Many rare genetic conditions lack effective treatments. For families affected, gene replacement therapy offers hope where none existed before. Advancements in Technology

Improvements in gene-editing tools, delivery systems, and safety methods have made the therapy more practical and accessible than ever before. How Does Gene Replacement Therapy Work? Step 1: Identifying the Faulty Gene

Doctors first determine which gene is causing the problem. Step 2: Delivering the Healthy Gene

A vector, often a modified virus, carries the healthy gene into the patient’s cells. Step 3: Restoring Function

Once inside, the new gene starts producing the correct proteins, helping the body function more normally. It’s a precise process, requiring strict safety protocols and expert handling. Inherited Disorders

Diseases like hemophilia, sickle cell anemia, and spinal muscular atrophy have shown promising responses to gene replacement therapy. Certain Cancers

Gene therapy has even restored partial sight in patients with inherited blindness. These examples highlight why so many researchers and patients are hopeful about this field. Challenges and Risks

While promising, gene replacement therapy is not without risks. Safety Concerns

Introducing new genes carries the possibility of immune reactions or unintended effects. Cost and Accessibility

Currently, the therapy is expensive, making it out of reach for many patients. Scaling up production and reducing costs remain major challenges. Long-Term Data

Because the field is relatively new, researchers are still studying long-term outcomes. This data is essential to understand safety and effectiveness over decades. Healthcare providers like Manaaki Healthcare emphasize careful screening and patient monitoring to manage these risks responsibly. The Future of Gene Replacement Therapy

Looking ahead, researchers aim to make therapies safer, cheaper, and more widely available. As more clinical trials succeed, we may see these treatments move from rare disorders to more common conditions. With growing collaboration between hospitals, biotech companies, and healthcare organizations, gene replacement therapy could soon become part of mainstream medicine. FAQs

Is gene replacement therapy a permanent cure? In some cases, yes. If the replaced gene continues to function correctly, it may provide long-lasting relief. However, results vary depending on the disease. 2. Who is eligible for gene replacement therapy? Eligibility depends on the condition, its genetic cause, and the patient’s overall health. Doctors usually conduct detailed tests before recommending it. 3. How safe is gene replacement therapy? It has shown encouraging results in trials, but like all treatments, it carries risks. Ongoing monitoring and research help improve safety standards. Conclusion

So, why is gene replacement therapy the buzzword in modern medicine? Because it shifts the focus from symptom management to tackling the genetic root of disease. From rare inherited disorders to certain cancers, it holds once unimaginable possibilities. Healthcare providers such as
